Neonates of the round disk snail (Discus rotundatus) emerge from their eggs with a shell breadth of just 0.1 cm [Lb = 0.1 cm], a dimension that reflects the limited calcium reserves available during early embryogenesis within the small, calcareous egg. Field surveys of populations in European deciduous forests indicate that this initial breadth is surprisingly consistent across microhabitats, likely due to strong constraints on egg size imposed by the need for the tiny hatchling to immediately begin rasping surface biofilm. At constant laboratory conditions of 21.5 °C [T = 21.5 °C], the period from egg deposition to emergence, representing the age at birth, averages 20 days [ab = 20 days], though the published range extends from 14 to 36 days depending on local thermal regimes and parental microhabitat selection. This incubation duration is comparatively brief among terrestrial pulmonates of similar adult dimensions, suggesting a strategy that prioritizes rapid entry into the juvenile feeding stage over extended embryonic provisioning. The synchronized emergence of siblings from a single egg mass is rarely observed; instead, staggered hatching over two to three days is typical, a pattern that may reduce intraspecific competition among neonates exploiting the same patch of leaf-litter fungi and algae during the critical first week of exogenous feeding.

As juvenile Discus rotundatus grow through successive instars, their shell breadth increases steadily until levelling off at the adult value of 0.65 cm [Li = 0.65 cm], a measurement that represents the ultimate shell breadth attained by fully grown individuals. This asymptotic dimension places the species among the smaller members of the family Discidae, though the relatively globose shell morphology confers a favorable surface-area-to-volume ratio for water conservation in the humid litter layer. The dry weight of a fully mature adult shell and body, after careful desiccation, reaches approximately 0.0052 grams , a remarkably low mass that underscores the species' reliance on a thin, translucent shell composed primarily of aragonite. This ultimate dry weight was estimated using a size-corrected allometric relationship derived from the larger land snail Cepaea nemoralis, adjusted for the proportional volume difference between a sphere of 0.65 centimeters versus one of 2.2 centimeters. The resulting value of 5.2 milligrams of dry tissue and shell is consistent with direct measurements of similarly sized European discid snails, confirming the utility of cross-species scaling for predicting mass in taxa where destructive sampling is impractical.

Reproductive maturity in Discus rotundatus is attained when the shell breadth reaches approximately 0.6 cm [Lp = approximately 0.6 cm], a threshold that coincides with the completion of the shell lip thickening characteristic of adult pulmonates. Individuals at this size are capable of copulation and subsequent egg production, though the transition from juvenile to sexually mature adult may span several weeks depending on food quality and temperature. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 21.5 °C [T = 21.5 °C], the lifetime reproductive output per individual has been quantified at 178 eggs , a cumulative figure that integrates multiple spawning events over the animal's reproductive lifespan. This total fecundity is modest compared to many terrestrial gastropods that produce hundreds or thousands of eggs annually, but it is consistent with a life-history strategy emphasizing relatively large, well-provisioned eggs rather than high fecundity. Each individual egg measures roughly 1.5 to 2.0 millimeters in diameter and contains sufficient yolk to support embryonic development through to the hatching stage without any maternal provisioning beyond oviposition.
